contract: build_model(data) -> (cpmpy.Model, extractor) written with CPMpy 0.10.1 (import cpmpy as cp); data keys n_cars, n_classes, n_options, quantity[c] (cars of class c), maxcars[o] and blksize[o] (at most maxcars[o] cars needing option o in any blksize[o] consecutive slots), usage[c][o] in {0, 1}; extractor() -> {'sequence': list of n_cars class indices}. Satisfaction models only (no objective); cpmpy, numpy and a small standard-library subset may be imported. Score (maximize): PAR2 runtime speedup over the baseline model on held-out generated satisfiable instances (fresh secret seeds in every evaluation, sizes as in the parameters) = sum of baseline seconds / sum of candidate seconds, where an instance's seconds are the CPU time of the model module's top-level code + build_model + CPMpy-to-OR-Tools transformation and export (in a sandboxed child process, measured from outside it) + CP-SAT Solve (1 worker, seed 42, separate process) + extractor (child), and an instance not finished within its cap (max(cap_floor, cap_factor x baseline)) counts 2 x cap; a wrong answer or an infeasibility claim makes the candidate invalid
notes: Car sequencing instances use five options with the classic CSPLib capacities 1/2, 2/3, 1/3, 2/5 and 1/5; class option sets and demands are derived from a planted random sequence that respects every window (generator generate_car_sequencing, 12 random option sets plus the empty one, bias toward option-heavy classes).

Instances: the paper draws AutoIG-generated pools (Spracklen et al. 2023), keeps satisfiable instances with baseline runtimes of 1-300 s and splits them 8/8/16 into training, validation and test sets; those pools are not released and are not reproduced. This task uses 8 locally generated satisfiable instances (generator arguments in the parameters; generators are deterministic SplitMix64 streams in or_csp_csplib.py), graded so that the baseline needs roughly 0.1-6 CPU seconds each on an Apple M-series CPU.

The scored instances are held out, as in the paper (which scores a held-out test split): every evaluation generates each instance from a fresh secret seed with the sizes given in the parameters, and keeps a draw only when the baseline solves it within 0.1-6 CPU seconds, the band the published seeds were picked from (parameter held_out; at most 8 draws per instance, an instance with no draw in the band is excluded). The published seeds show what the instances look like and are not scored. The drawn seeds are reported in the result's per_instance rows, so any evaluation can be rebuilt. Because the instances change, scores vary more between evaluations than on a fixed set, and the baseline draws add up to about a minute to an evaluation.

Runtime measure: CPU seconds of the model module's top-level code + build_model + CPMpy 0.10.1 transformation to OR-Tools + export of the transformed model in protobuf text format (all in a sandboxed child process, a fresh one per instance and model, whose CPU clock the evaluator reads from outside when the child reports each step) + CP-SAT Solve (OR-Tools 9.14.6206, one search worker, random seed 42, in a separate clean process) + extractor (in the child; any CPU the child uses while the solver runs counts here too). The baseline goes through the same path. Compared with the earlier in-process measurement, the module's top-level code and the text export now count (the export is about 5% of the baselines' build time); a model whose build or extractor does not finish within the cap is stopped and counts 2 x cap. The paper reports solving time (time to first solution) without saying whether it is wall-clock or CPU time or whether model construction and the CPMpy transformation count (CPMpy 0.10.1 and CP-SAT with one search worker, up to eight concurrent single-core runs on an Intel Core i7-12700, Section 5; seed 42, Appendix A; a 300 s per-instance limit, Appendix B), so counting build and transformation time here may itself differ from the paper. CP-SAT's deterministic time is not used: it excludes presolve work (instances closed in presolve report 0) and its work units are not comparable across constraint types. CPU time has run-to-run noise of about 1% on an idle machine and more under load; scores are ratios measured on the same machine in the same evaluation.

Score: sum of baseline seconds / sum of candidate seconds over the instances (the paper's per-run speedup T_S(B)/T_S(m) with PAR2); an instance not finished within its cap of max(cap_floor, cap_factor x baseline seconds) = max(1 s, 3 x baseline) counts 2 x cap. The paper uses a fixed 300 s per-instance limit and, during search, caps the total training evaluation at C_B = max(T_B, min(1.5 T_B, 900)) s (Section 5); no such cap is applied here. The per-instance geometric-mean speedup is reported in the details.

Validity: the paper accepts an answer when fixing it into the baseline model leaves it satisfiable; here an independent checker of the CSPLib definition verifies every answer (equivalent when the baseline is correct). A wrong answer, a claim that an instance is infeasible, an objective, a model OR-Tools rejects, or an import outside cpmpy, numpy and a standard-library allowlist makes the candidate invalid (the import and dunder-attribute checks are guards, kept as defence in depth). The module's top-level code, build_model and the extractor run only in the sandboxed child process (audit-hook policy, CPU, wall-clock and memory limits; the candidate is never imported by the evaluator); the evaluator solves the model the child sends, checks the answer and measures the child's CPU time in its own processes, so model code cannot reach the scoring. The sandbox is defence in depth for honest model search, not a boundary against hostile native code. A transformed model with an objective, a solution hint, a search strategy, symmetry information or assumptions, or a child that breaks the message protocol, is invalid. Only the answers are verified, not how they were obtained; answers stored for the published seeds do not help, because the scored instances are drawn fresh in every evaluation.

Baseline: a local direct translation of the CSPLib Essence model (github.com/csplib/csplib, Problems/probNNN/models/*.essence); the paper's baseline models are not released. The baseline is remeasured in every evaluation, as in the paper.

Candidates follow the PDR paper's contract (CPMpy build_model(data) -> (model, extractor), same answer structure as the baseline). The baseline is a local translation of the problem's CSPLib model (for covering arrays, of the baseline printed in the paper); instances are chosen locally and every answer is verified by an independent checker of the CSPLib definition.
protocol_description: Locally implemented or adapted evaluator for the cited task or benchmark. Data sources, generated instances, evaluation budgets and protocol differences are specified in the candidate contract, requirements and notes; scores are not automatically comparable with published results.
